title: Your Bank Pays 0.01% — Here's the Legal Fix
caption: Big banks pay 0.01% while online banks pay 400x more. Sources: FDIC, Bankrate 2026. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for researched money tips.
lines: Your bank is paying you ten cents a year to hold a thousand dollars. Not a typo.
Chase, Bank of America, U.S. Bank. Their standard savings rate is zero point zero one percent.
Meanwhile, FDIC-insured online banks are paying around four percent. Same insurance. Same money. Four hundred times the interest.
On ten thousand dollars, that's the difference between one dollar a year and four hundred.
The banks bet you'll never move it. Most people don't. Twenty minutes to open a high-yield account beats a year of work raises.
Look up high-yield savings accounts tonight. Your money should be working the night shift.

title: 1 in 4 Workers Refuse Free Money Every Month
caption: The average worker skipping their 401k match loses $1,336/year — $43,000 over 20 years. Source: Financial Engines study. Follow @moneyrewired.daily.
lines: One in four workers turns down free money from their boss every single month.
It's the 401k match. Your employer offers to match what you put in, up to a limit.
Skip it, and the average worker loses over thirteen hundred dollars a year. Researchers found twenty-four billion dollars goes unclaimed annually.
With compounding, one worker's missed match can grow past forty thousand dollars in twenty years.
A match is a guaranteed one hundred percent return. No stock on earth promises that.
Tomorrow, ask HR one question. What do I contribute to get the full match? Then set it.

title: You Think You Spend $86 on Subscriptions. Try $219.
caption: Americans underestimate subscription spending by 2.5x. Ten minutes tonight = hundreds back. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for researched money tips.
lines: Quick. How much do you spend on subscriptions per month? Got a number?
Surveys say the average guess is about eighty-six dollars. The real average? Two hundred nineteen.
People underestimate by two and a half times. Because subscriptions are designed to be forgotten.
Sixty percent of people pay for at least one they don't even use.
Here's the ten minute fix. Open your bank app. Search last month for every recurring charge. Cancel anything you wouldn't re-buy today.
Most people find two hundred dollars a year hiding in there. That's a car payment.
Follow, then go do the audit. Seriously. Tonight.

title: The 15-Minute Phone Call That Pays $300+
caption: Bill negotiation succeeds up to 90% of the time — most people never try. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for researched money tips.
lines: There's a phone call that pays three to eight hundred dollars an hour. Almost nobody makes it.
Professional bill negotiators report success rates near ninety percent on internet and phone bills. Ninety.
That means the price you're paying is basically the no-thank-you price.
The script is simple. Call, say you're considering canceling, and ask for the retention department. Then ask what promotions they can apply.
Internet alone typically drops ten to forty dollars a month. That's up to four hundred eighty a year for fifteen minutes of hold music.
Works on cable, phone, insurance, even many medical bills. The worst case is they say no.

title: The Tiny Label That Cuts Grocery Bills 20%+
caption: Unit pricing + store brands = the researched way to slash groceries without coupons. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for money tips with sources.
lines: There's a number on every shelf tag that most shoppers never read. It's costing them twenty percent or more.
It's the unit price. The cost per ounce, hidden in small print under the big price.
The big price lies. A bigger box can cost less per ounce. A sale item can cost more.
Shoppers who compare unit prices spend twenty to thirty-seven percent less on the same items. Nielsen data.
And one more move. A 2026 study of a hundred seventy-one products found store brands run up to seventy-five percent cheaper. Often made in the same factories.
Small print, big money. Read the shelf tag, not the sticker.

title: Your Credit Card Charges 22%. Attack It Like This.
caption: Average card APR is ~22%. The avalanche method clears debt faster and cheaper. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for researched money tips.
lines: The average credit card now charges about twenty-two percent interest. Let that sink in.
The average balance is around sixty-five hundred dollars. At that rate, minimum payments mostly feed the interest monster.
Here's the method the math loves. The avalanche.
List every debt by interest rate. Pay minimums on everything. Throw every spare dollar at the highest rate first.
Compared to paying off small balances first, the avalanche saves hundreds in interest and months of payments. Same money, better order.
There is no investment that reliably beats paying off a twenty-two percent debt. None.
Follow for the debt math banks hope you never run.

title: Loyalty to Your Car Insurance Costs $694/Year
caption: Drivers who re-shop their policy save $694/year on average — some save $1,370. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for researched money tips.
lines: Staying loyal to your car insurance company has a price. About six hundred ninety-four dollars a year.
That's the average saving for drivers who re-shop their policy, according to industry studies. Some save over thirteen hundred.
Insurers count on inertia. Rates creep up at renewal because most people just... pay.
It even has a name. The loyalty penalty.
The fix takes twenty minutes a year. Get three quotes before every renewal. Then either switch, or call your insurer with the competitor's number.
Same coverage. Same car. Hundreds back. Every year.
Follow. Your renewal notice is not a bill, it's an opening offer.

title: Why Lottery Winners Always End Up Broke
caption: Winning millions doesn't fix a broke mindset. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Seventy percent of lottery winners end up broke. Here's why.
Your brain has a thermostat for happiness. It's called hedonic adaptation.
Win ten million dollars, and within a year, your brain feels exactly like before.
So winners chase the high. Bigger house. Faster car. Until it's gone.
Wealth isn't what you win. It's what you keep doing every single day.

title: The Price Tag Trick Stores Use on Your Brain
caption: That 'sale' price was designed in a lab. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: That jacket was never four hundred dollars. Here's the trick.
It's called anchoring. The first number you see becomes your reference point.
Two hundred feels cheap next to four hundred. Even if it was always worth two hundred.
Stores invented the fake original price just to plant that anchor.
Next time, ask one question. Would I pay this if I never saw the other number?
Follow for the tricks your brain falls for every day.

title: Why Losing $100 Hurts More Than Winning $100
caption: Your brain counts losses double. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Losing a hundred dollars hurts twice as much as winning a hundred feels good.
Scientists call it loss aversion. And it quietly runs your money life.
It's why you hold losing stocks, hoping they'll come back.
It's why you keep the gym membership you never use. Canceling feels like admitting the loss.
Rich people cut losses fast. They know a small loss now beats a big one later.
Follow for more brain hacks your wallet will thank you for.

title: Why One Purchase Always Turns Into Ten
caption: New shoes demand a new outfit. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Ever buy one thing, then suddenly need ten more? That's not an accident.
It's the Diderot effect. Named after a philosopher who ruined himself over a bathrobe.
He got a fancy new robe. Then his desk looked shabby next to it. Then his chair. Then everything.
One upgrade makes everything around it feel outdated. So you keep buying.
The fix? Before upgrading anything, ask what else it will drag with it.
Follow so your brain stops spending your paycheck.

title: Why Rich People Look Poor and Poor People Look Rich
caption: Real wealth is invisible. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: The guy in the old t-shirt might be worth millions. The guy in the Lamborghini might be broke.
Here's the psychology. Spending money on status is how you signal wealth you don't have.
Actual wealth is what you don't see. The investments. The savings. The paid-off house.
Every dollar spent looking rich is a dollar not making you rich.
Stop buying the costume. Build the character.
Follow for the money truths nobody posts about.

title: Why Your Raise Disappeared
caption: Expenses rise to meet income — unless you stop them. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Got a raise last year? So where is it?
Parkinson's law. Expenses rise to meet income. Automatically. Silently.
Make more, spend more. The bigger apartment. The nicer car. It never feels like a choice.
That's why people earning six figures still live paycheck to paycheck.
The fix. When income goes up, raise your savings rate first. Then live on the rest.
Follow for more. Your future self is watching.

title: Why You Spend Money When You're Sad
caption: Sadness makes you pay more — literally. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Sad people pay up to three hundred percent more for the same item. Real study.
Sadness makes you feel a loss of control. Buying something gives it back. For about ten minutes.
That's why it's called retail therapy. Except the therapy wears off and the bill doesn't.
Stores know this. Ever notice ads that make you feel behind in life? That's the setup.
Feeling down? Wait twenty-four hours before buying anything over fifty dollars.
Follow for the psychology tricks hiding in your bank statement.

title: Why Billionaires Wear the Same Outfit Every Day
caption: Every choice costs brainpower. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Steve Jobs. Same black turtleneck. Every single day. It wasn't a fashion choice.
Your brain makes about thirty-five thousand decisions a day. And each one drains the battery.
It's called decision fatigue. By evening, your willpower is running on empty.
That's when you order takeout, impulse buy, and skip the gym.
Automate the small stuff. Same breakfast. Auto-pay. Auto-savings. Save your brain for decisions that pay.

title: The Mindset Loop That Keeps People Poor
caption: Scarcity taxes your brain. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Being broke literally makes it harder to think. That's science, not an insult.
Researchers found money stress drops effective IQ by about thirteen points.
When your brain is consumed by this month's rent, it can't plan next year's escape.
That's the scarcity trap. Poverty creates stress. Stress creates bad decisions. Bad decisions create poverty.
Breaking it starts small. One automated transfer. Even five dollars. It gives your brain proof of progress.
Follow. Because understanding the trap is how you exit it.

title: Why 'Free' Costs You the Most Money
caption: Nothing is more expensive than free. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: The most expensive word in marketing is free.
Free sample. Free trial. Free shipping over fifty dollars. All engineered.
It's called reciprocity. Your brain feels a debt when it gets something free. So you buy.
And free shipping? People spend thirty percent more just to avoid a five dollar fee.
Rule of thumb. If it's free, you're not the customer. Your wallet is the product.

title: The Gym Membership You Can't Cancel (Psychology)
caption: Stop paying for your past decisions. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: You haven't been to the gym in four months. You're still paying. Why?
Sunk cost fallacy. Canceling feels like admitting the money was wasted.
But here's the truth. That money is gone whether you cancel or not.
The only question that matters is, would you sign up again today? No? Cancel.
Do a subscription audit tonight. Most people find over a hundred dollars a month in zombie payments.

title: The 24-Hour Rule That Kills Impulse Buying
caption: Your cart can wait a day. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: One weird rule saves people thousands a year. Wait twenty-four hours.
Impulse buys happen because desire peaks the moment you see the thing.
Dopamine floods your brain, and it feels like you need it. But dopamine has a half-life.
Sleep on it once, and most of that wanting just evaporates.
Put it in the cart. Close the app. If you still want it tomorrow, buy it guilt-free.

title: Why Credit Cards Make You Spend 30% More
caption: Plastic turns off the pain. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Paying with a card makes you spend about thirty percent more. Here's the science.
Handing over cash activates the same brain regions as physical pain. Really.
Cards remove that pain. Tap. Done. Your brain never registers the loss.
Casinos figured this out first. That's why you play with chips, not cash.
Try one cash-only week. Watching money physically leave changes everything.

title: Lifestyle Creep: The Silent Raise Killer
caption: You don't need a bigger life. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: You make more money than ever. So why are you still broke?
Lifestyle creep. Every raise quietly upgrades your normal.
Coffee becomes lattes. The apartment gets a gym. Old you would call new you rich.
But your savings rate? Exactly where it was five years ago.
Here's the rule. Celebrate the raise once. Then bank half of it forever. You still feel richer, and you actually get richer.

title: Why Knowing Your Coworker's Salary Ruins Your Day
caption: Comparison is a pay cut for your happiness. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Would you rather earn fifty thousand where everyone makes forty, or sixty thousand where everyone makes eighty?
Most people pick the fifty. Read that again.
Your brain doesn't measure money in dollars. It measures it in rank.
That's social comparison. And social media turned it into a twenty-four seven salary leaderboard.
The only comparison that builds wealth is you versus you, last year.

title: Why You Can't Sell Your Old Stuff
caption: Ownership inflates value. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Your old couch is worth two hundred dollars. You listed it for six hundred. Why?
The endowment effect. Owning something makes your brain inflate its value.
In experiments, people demanded twice as much to sell a mug as they'd pay to buy the same mug.
It's why garages stay full and side hustles stay unsold.
Price things at what you'd actually pay, not what they mean to you. Stuff moves. Cash flows.

title: Why Tax Refunds Get Wasted (But Paychecks Don't)
caption: Money is money — your brain disagrees. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: A thousand dollar tax refund gets blown. A thousand dollar paycheck gets budgeted. Same money. Why?
Mental accounting. Your brain files money into invisible buckets.
Refunds, bonuses, birthday cash. They land in the fun bucket. So they vanish.
But every dollar spends exactly the same.
Trick your brain back. The moment surprise money lands, move it to savings before it gets a label.

title: The Most Expensive Sentence in English
caption: 'I deserve this' costs thousands a year. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: The most expensive sentence in the English language? I deserve this.
It's called moral licensing. Do something good, and your brain issues itself a permission slip.
Worked hard all week? Treat yourself. Went to the gym? Earned that dessert. Saved money? Spend some.
One study found people spend more right after doing something virtuous.
You do deserve nice things. You also deserve to not be broke. Pick rewards that don't undo the work.

title: Why Get-Rich Stories Are Lies (Survivorship Bias)
caption: You only hear from the winners. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: College dropout becomes billionaire. Great story. Terrible advice.
It's survivorship bias. You only hear from the ones who made it.
For every dropout billionaire, a million dropouts are just... dropouts. They don't get documentaries.
Same with crypto bros and day traders. The losers delete their accounts quietly.
Before copying anyone's path, ask, where are the people this didn't work for?

title: Automation Beats Willpower Every Time
caption: Stop relying on discipline. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: People who automate savings save four times more. Not because they're disciplined.
Willpower is a battery. Stress, work, and decisions drain it daily.
Relying on willpower to save means betting on your most tired self.
Automation removes the decision entirely. The money moves before you're even awake.
Set one automatic transfer for payday morning. Any amount. Your brain adapts to what's left.

title: The 1% Rule That Builds Quiet Wealth
caption: Tiny habits compound. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Getting one percent better at money each week doesn't sound like much. It's everything.
Compounding isn't just for investments. It works on habits too.
One percent more saved. One subscription cut. One impulse skipped. Each one seems pointless.
But stack fifty-two tiny wins, and your finances become unrecognizable in a year.
Don't aim for a money makeover. Aim for one small win this week.

title: Your Friends' Spending Becomes Your Spending
caption: Wealth is contagious. So is broke. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Your bank account looks like the average of your five closest friends'. Uncomfortable? Keep watching.
Humans mirror their group. Spending habits spread like accents.
If brunch, bottle service, and new fits are the group norm, your brain treats them as baseline.
Nobody's saying ditch your friends.
Just notice which habits are actually yours, and which ones you absorbed.

title: Why Checking Your Investments Daily Loses You Money
caption: Watch less, earn more. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: The more you check your investments, the worse they perform. Here's why.
Markets wobble daily. And thanks to loss aversion, every dip hurts double.
Check daily, and you'll feel pain most days, even in a good year.
Pain triggers action. Selling low. Chasing winners. Exactly the wrong moves.
The best investors act like they forgot their password.

title: The Overconfidence Tax on Day Traders
caption: Confidence isn't a strategy. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Ninety percent of day traders lose money. Every one of them thought they'd be the exception.
That's the overconfidence effect. We all think we're above average. Statistically impossible.
Markets are where overconfidence goes to get expensive.
The pros? They assume they're wrong constantly and build in safety nets.
Boring, consistent investing beats exciting trading for almost everyone. The data is brutal on this.

title: Why Round Numbers Cost You in Negotiations
caption: Ask for $73,400, not $70k. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Asking for seventy thousand gets you less than asking for seventy-three thousand four hundred. Weird but true.
Round numbers sound like guesses. Precise numbers sound like research.
Studies show precise first offers get significantly better outcomes.
The other side assumes you know something they don't. So they push back less.
Next negotiation, bring a weirdly specific number and a straight face.

title: FOMO: The Most Expensive Emotion
caption: Missing out is usually free. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: The most expensive emotion in finance isn't greed. It's the fear of missing out.
FOMO hijacks the same brain circuits as physical thirst. You don't decide. You grab.
It's why people buy stocks at the top and concert tickets at triple price.
Here's the reframe. There will always be another opportunity. Always.
The person who missed the last hype train and kept their cash? They're fine. Better than fine.

title: Why 'Saving What's Left' Never Works
caption: There's never anything left. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Plan to save whatever's left at the end of the month? There's never anything left.
Parkinson's law strikes again. Spending expands to fill available money.
Your brain sees the balance and calibrates spending to it. Automatically.
Flip the order. Savings leaves the account the morning you're paid. You budget from what remains.
Same income. Same life. Completely different outcome in five years.

title: Companies Profit From Your Laziness (The Default Effect)
caption: Defaults decide your money. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Companies make billions from one psychological trick. The default.
Auto-renew. Pre-checked boxes. Opt-out instead of opt-in. Whatever the default is, ninety percent of people keep it.
Changing anything takes effort, and your brain avoids effort like it's poison.
But defaults cut both ways.
Make saving your default. Auto-transfer, auto-invest, auto-pay. Then laziness builds wealth instead of draining it.

title: Experiences Beat Stuff (Except When They Don't)
caption: Buy memories, not clutter — mostly. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Science says experiences make you happier than stuff. But there's a catch nobody mentions.
Stuff fades into the background. The new phone is exciting for a week, then it's just your phone.
Experiences become part of your identity. And they improve with retelling.
The catch? Anticipation is half the joy. Booked trips beat impulse trips.
And one exception. Stuff that buys back your time, like a dishwasher, beats almost everything.

title: Why Expensive Feels Better (Even When It Isn't)
caption: The price changes the taste. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Same wine. Two labels. One says ten dollars, one says ninety. People swear the ninety tastes better.
Brain scans prove it. The pleasure centers literally light up more for the expensive label.
Price creates a halo. Expensive equals better, says your brain, before you even try it.
Brands charge more partly because the high price itself is the product.
Blind test your favorites once. Coffee, wine, skincare. The results will save you thousands.

title: Financial Stress Makes You Worse With Money
caption: The cruelest money trap. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Here's the cruelest thing about money problems. They make you worse at solving them.
Scientists call it the bandwidth tax. Financial stress occupies your mental RAM.
With your brain busy surviving today, planning tomorrow becomes nearly impossible.
This isn't a character flaw. It's biology. Anyone under money stress decides worse.
So automate before the storm. Systems you build on good days protect you on bad ones.
Follow for money psychology with zero judgment.

title: The Trade Rich People Make Differently
caption: Time is the only currency you can't earn back. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Poor people trade time for money. Rich people trade money for time. Cliché, but the data backs it.
People who spend money to save time report higher happiness at every income level. Every level.
Yet most of us drive across town to save five dollars while our hourly worth sits at thirty.
Calculate your real hourly rate. Then run every errand and side gig against it.
Sometimes the frugal choice is the expensive one.
Follow for the math your calendar wants you to see.

title: The 'Buy Now Pay Later' Brain Trap
caption: Four easy payments. One expensive habit. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Four easy payments of twenty-five dollars sounds harmless. Your brain thinks it's four twenty-five dollar items.
That's payment partitioning. Splitting a price makes it register as smaller. Much smaller.
Buy now pay later users spend more per purchase and default more often. That's the whole business model.
You're not borrowing money. You're borrowing from a version of you who is somehow richer. They're not.
If you can't buy it once, don't buy it four times.
Follow before your next checkout screen tempts you.

title: Why More Options Make You Buy Worse Things
caption: Choice overload is real. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: A store offered twenty-four jams. Then just six. The smaller table sold ten times more.
That's the paradox of choice. Too many options paralyze your brain.
And when overloaded, you either freeze, or grab whatever's most heavily advertised.
Marketers know this. Endless options push you toward their sponsored pick.
Decide your criteria before you shop. Three requirements. First option that hits all three wins.

title: Status Games: The Invisible Tax on Your Income
caption: You can't win a game with no finish line. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: There's a tax nobody talks about. The status tax.
It's every dollar spent to look successful instead of to be comfortable.
The badge car. The logo bag. The right zip code. All payments toward an image.
Here's the brutal part. The audience you're performing for is too busy performing to notice.
Opting out of status games is the biggest raise most people will ever give themselves.
Follow if you're ready to stop paying it.

title: The Latte Factor Is a Lie (Kind Of)
caption: It was never about the coffee. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Skip your daily latte and become a millionaire. You've heard it. It's mostly wrong.
Five dollars a day invested for forty years is real money, sure. But that's not why you're broke.
The big three decide your finances. Housing. Transportation. Food. That's seventy percent of most budgets.
Optimizing pennies while ignoring the big three is financial theater.
Drive a modest car and win the housing decision, and you can buy all the lattes you want.
Follow for money advice with a sense of proportion.

title: Why Effort Makes You Overpay (The IKEA Effect)
caption: You love it because you built it. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: People value furniture they assembled themselves sixty-three percent higher. Same furniture.
It's the IKEA effect. Effort creates attachment. Attachment inflates value.
Companies exploit it constantly. Customize your sneakers. Build your bundle. Design your box.
The moment you invest effort, your brain marks up the price.
Notice when a checkout flow makes you work. That labor is the sales tactic.

title: Your First Salary Follows You Forever
caption: Negotiate early — the anchor is real. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Your first salary quietly decides your next ten. Here's how.
Every raise is a percentage of your current number. Every job offer anchors to your last one.
Start five thousand low, and the gap compounds like interest, in reverse.
This is why negotiating your first offer matters more than any raise after.
And if you started low? A job switch is the only reliable anchor reset. Switchers out-earn stayers.

title: Why Budgets Fail (And What Works Instead)
caption: Stop budgeting. Start automating. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Budgets fail for the same reason diets fail. Restriction psychology.
Track every dollar, feel guilty about each purchase, burn out by February.
Your willpower can't run a spreadsheet forever. It was never designed to.
What works? Automation plus one simple rule. Savings first, bills second, and whatever's left is guilt-free.
No categories. No tracking apps. No shame spiral. Just a system that runs itself.

title: The Money Beliefs You Inherited From Your Parents
caption: Your money habits were programmed before age 7. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Your money habits were mostly programmed before you turned seven. Psychologists call them money scripts.
Money doesn't grow on trees. Rich people are greedy. We can't afford that. Sound familiar?
These childhood phrases become adult behavior. Avoidance. Worship. Hoarding. Status spending.
You can't delete a script you've never read.
Write down three things your family always said about money. That's your source code. Now you can edit it.
Follow to keep rewiring, one script at a time.

title: The Happiness Treadmill Eating Your Paycheck
caption: The high always fades. The bill doesn't. Follow @moneyrewired.daily for daily money psychology.
lines: Remember how happy your last big purchase made you? Neither do you.
The hedonic treadmill. Every upgrade becomes the new normal within weeks.
So you buy again, chasing a feeling that keeps moving the finish line.
Marketers don't sell products. They sell the fifteen minutes before the feeling fades.
Gratitude sounds cheesy, but it's literally the off switch. Wanting what you have is free.
Follow for the psychology of enough.
